clue.text: Affectionate little creatures, sweet little things

parts.note: fond means affectionate
ants are small insects, little creatures

explanation.surface: Someone describes dear little animals and other sweet little things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affectionate little creatures' reads as one phrase about pets, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: These are soft sugary confections, small sweets often with a creamy centre.

clue.text: Energy source brings befuddlement, but it's no con

indicators.note: 'it's no con' tells us the word con is to be absent from the longer word

parts.note: befuddlement is a state of confusion
taken as written

explanation.surface: An energy source baffles people but is said to be no swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'con' looks like a swindle but is just its three letters, removed from the front of the word for befuddlement.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuclear joining of light atoms releases power, as in the sun and in hoped-for reactors.

clue.text: Fresh fellow said to be in cell

indicators.note: said to be signals that the pieces before it are spoken aloud rather than spelt

parts.note: fresh means new; Ron is a man's name, standing for any fellow

explanation.surface: A new man is reported to be locked in a prison cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cell' suggests a prison, but it is the biological kind found in the brain and nerves.
explanation.definitionFit: A nerve cell carries electrical signals through the nervous system.

clue.text: Hearing statement of independence embraced by a politician

indicators.note: embraced by means held inside the other pieces, as in arms

parts.note: taken as written
a Tory is a British Conservative politician
UDI is the Unilateral Declaration of Independence, made by Rhodesia in 1965

explanation.surface: A politician hugs a declaration of independence at a hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' looks like a noun for a court session, but the definition is the adjective meaning relating to the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything to do with the ear or the sense of sound.

clue.text: Flimsy item that's no good

indicators.note: 'that's no good' tells us the letter for good is dropped from the word

parts.note: a thing is an item

explanation.surface: Something flimsy turns out to be an item of no use.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe material lacking substance or thickness, easily torn.

clue.text: Found at the end of the month, a very old sort of book

indicators.note: found at the end of says the following pieces come after the month

parts.note: Oct is short for October
taken as written

explanation.surface: A very old book is discovered at the end of the month.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Found at the end of the month' as placing A, V and O after OCT, not as a date.
explanation.definitionFit: A book size made by folding each printed sheet three times into eight leaves.

clue.text: Confirm 150 in church

parts.note: CL is 150 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A congregation of 150 confirms something in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a container signal but just gives its own letters; 'Confirm' suggests the church rite but means seal a deal, as in clinching a sale.
explanation.definitionFit: To seal or settle a deal decisively, as in finally securing an agreement.

clue.text: Everyone joining a nice new union

parts.note: all means everyone

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of the words are made fresh, rearranged

explanation.surface: Everybody signs up to a pleasant new trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' looks like an adjective on 'union', but it rearranges A NICE into IANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pact or coalition joining parties together for a shared purpose.

clue.text: Old-fashioned mood duet conjured up

indicators.note: conjured up suggests letters magically transformed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A magician conjures up a dated, sentimental duet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something no longer in style or current use is out of date.

clue.text: Soldier in side running around courtyard

indicators.note: around means the rearranged letters surround the courtyard word
running suggests the letters move about into a new order

parts.note: a quad is a quadrangle, a college courtyard

explanation.surface: A soldier on a team runs around a courtyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'side' looks like a team, but its letters are the fodder; 'running' rearranges them into S...DIE. 'Squaddie' is British army slang.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a private in the army, a rank-and-file serviceman.

clue.text: Risk getting hold of bad accommodation

indicators.note: getting hold of means the first word grips the second inside it

parts.note: to bet is to risk money
ill means bad

explanation.surface: Someone takes a chance on poor lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: Lodging assigned to soldiers, often in a private house.

clue.text: Runner possibly allowed to enter reorganised heat

indicators.note: to enter means the word for allowed goes inside the other letters
reorganised means the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: let means allowed

explanation.surface: A runner is permitted to enter a rescheduled heat of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heat' looks like a race round, fitting 'Runner', but it is fodder: 'reorganised' gives ATHE. 'possibly' marks the definition as one example among many sports.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner is one example of a sports competitor, hence 'possibly'.

clue.text: Left in the middle of wood somewhere in Portugal

indicators.note: in means the word for left goes inside the middle letters
the middle of means only the central letters of the word are used

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone is abandoned deep in a forest somewhere in Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb (abandoned), but it is the nautical side.
explanation.definitionFit: An English name for Porto, the city in northern Portugal famous for its fortified wine.

clue.text: One pussy about to get another, coming in so jerkily

indicators.note: coming in means the cats go inside the word so

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about tells us the first cat is turned round

parts.note: a pussy is a cat
another pussy, so another cat

explanation.surface: One cat turns to fetch another, both coming indoors in fits and starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pussy' is just a cat; 'about' turns the first one round to TAC. 'jerkily' fits the musical sense of short, detached notes.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical term for notes played short and detached from each other.

clue.text: With seas tossing around I am left drifting

indicators.note: around means the tossed letters surround the other pieces
tossing suggests the letters are thrown about into a new order

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm

explanation.surface: Cast adrift on stormy seas, I am left floating about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tossing' gives AESS from the sea word, and the picture of a boat on rough water hides that 'drifting' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Wandering without purpose or direction, like a boat with no course.

clue.text: Maybe the recital can be rearranged

indicators.note: can be rearranged openly signals that the letters of the word are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a concert could be rescheduled.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the tiny word 'the', an example of a grammatical part of speech, hence 'Maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word 'the' is the definite one of the grammatical determiners in English.

clue.text: Bill wants yours truly to be top

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
yours truly is a jokey way of saying me

explanation.surface: Bill wants to be the best himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is an invoice or account.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point or peak of achievement.

clue.text: This funny fellow entertaining one in ancient Corinth

indicators.note: funny suggests the letters are behaving oddly, out of order
entertaining means holding the other piece inside, as a host does

parts.note: a man is a fellow
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A comic fellow hosts a guest in ancient Corinth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funny' rearranges THIS into ISTH; MAN then holds I. The definition refers to the Isthmus of Corinth, home of the ancient Isthmian Games.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to the narrow land bridge of Corinth, where Greek games were held.

clue.text: Performed play, in charge like a teacher

parts.note: did means performed
an act is a performance or part of a play

explanation.surface: A teacher stages a performance and takes charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Intended to instruct, often in a lecturing or moralising manner.

clue.text: Cupboard to put bully in?

parts.note: bully here is bully beef, tinned corned beef, so this is a ventilated cupboard for storing food, not a place for a thug

explanation.surface: Somewhere to lock away a playground tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bully' suggests a thug, but bully beef is corned beef, kept in a mesh-fronted larder cupboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A ventilated cabinet for keeping cooked food cool and away from flies.

clue.text: Captain may have got a load of rubbish!

definitions.text: may have got a load of rubbish

explanation.surface: A captain may have received a lot of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: A rubbish container on a building site in Britain is called by this name; it also means a team captain, in curling or bowls especially.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a team leader's title and also a large open waste container delivered by lorry.

clue.text: Silly talk makes British foam

parts.note: lather is foam, as from soap

explanation.surface: Foolish chatter makes a British person froth.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-winded nonsense or idle chatter.

clue.text: Ploy's Richard's used after short time

definitions.note: read as the plural ploys, ignoring the apostrophe

indicators.note: after means the possessive name comes after the letter for time

parts.note: T is the short form of time
Rick is short for Richard, so Rick's is Richard's

explanation.surface: A ploy by Richard is used after a short time.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is read as the plural 'ploys'; the apostrophe belongs only to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Ploys are schemes or stratagems meant to deceive or outwit.

clue.text: The allure of a skin from what we hear

indicators.note: from what we hear tells us the words are spoken aloud

parts.note: a peel, the skin of a fruit

explanation.surface: The attraction of a fruit's skin, by all accounts.
explanation.definitionFit: Attractiveness or charm that draws people in.

clue.text: The man caught with pile of rocks is a bully

parts.note: he is the man
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
a tor is a rocky outcrop on a hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: The man caught with a heap of stones is a thug.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, a blustering person who browbeats others; also the verb for intimidating.

clue.text: The man trades abroad — gets top support

parts.note: he is the man

indicators.note: abroad suggests the letters are scattered widely, out of place

explanation.surface: A man trades overseas and gets the highest backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' rearranges TRADES into ADREST.
explanation.definitionFit: A cushion on a seat that props up the back of the head.

clue.text: Walk and exercise needed, that's plain

parts.note: a step is a pace in walking
PE is physical education, exercise

explanation.surface: A walk and some exercise are needed, that's obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plain' looks like the adjective meaning obvious, but it is a flat grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: A vast treeless grassland, especially in Russia and Central Asia.

clue.text: Sea bird spotted in Severn estuary

indicators.note: spotted in signals letters seen tucked inside the following words

explanation.surface: A sea bird is seen in the mouth of the Severn, a British river.
explanation.definitionFit: A white-tailed eagle that lives along coasts.

clue.text: International deed all there still

parts.note: an act is a deed

explanation.surface: An international action is still complete.
explanation.definitionFit: Undamaged and complete, with nothing missing.

clue.text: Decoration that's 'the last word' sadly torn on the outside

indicators.note: on the outside means the rearranged letters wrap around the other piece
sadly suggests the letters are in a sorry state, jumbled

parts.note: amen is the final word of a prayer

explanation.surface: A decoration is the final word in style, sadly ripped on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' gives ORNT; 'the last word' is the quoted phrase for the closing word of a prayer, not a judgment on fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorative object or trinket used to adorn something.

clue.text: Most pleasant French resort with short street

parts.note: Nice is a resort on the French Riviera
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: The loveliest French resort has a little street.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlative of an adjective meaning agreeable or kind.

clue.text: Radical measure introduced by crank?

indicators.note: introduced by means the measure is put inside the word for crank

parts.note: a crank handle works like a lever
an ell is an old measure of cloth length

explanation.surface: A radical policy brought in by an eccentric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crank' suggests an eccentric person, but here it is a lever. The Levellers were radicals in the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: One who seeks to abolish social distinctions, like the radical Civil War movement.
